title: The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

sheetTitle.es: La compra de Luisiana y el Cuerpo de Descubrimiento, 1803–1806

summary: Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.
subject: History
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map sets the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 beside the land the United States already held, and follows the Corps of Discovery's route, about 4,900 miles from Pittsburgh to the mouth of the Columbia River, with its approximate campsites. Two layers, off when the map opens, show today's biomes and river basins along the route (modern reference data, not a historical reconstruction).
bookmarks: Across the Rockies to the Pacific

layers.name: Territorial acquisitions to 1803
layers.shows: The land Britain gave up in 1783 (green) and the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 (yellow). Edges of the purchase that were settled later are in other colors or stripes: with Britain in 1818, and with Texas in 1845 and the Mexican Cession in 1848. Each pop-up gives a short note.

layers.name: Biomes
layers.shows: Today's biomes, shaded by type; each pop-up names the biome (first line), the realm and the ecoregion (a modern reference layer, not a historical reconstruction).

layers.name: United States Watersheds
layers.shows: River basins outlined in brown, from the 22 largest regions (Hydrologic Unit Code 2s, such as Ohio Region and Missouri Region) down to small watersheds as you zoom in; each pop-up names the basin and lists the states it touches (a modern reference layer, not a historical reconstruction).
layers.source: U.S. Geological Survey Watershed Boundary Dataset, via Esri (MapMaker catalogue)

layers.name: Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail
layers.shows: The National Park Service's line of the expedition's route, about 4,900 miles from Pittsburgh to the mouth of the Columbia River. No pop-up: the line has no information to click.
layers.source: National Park Service, Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail

layers.name: Lewis and Clark campsites (approximate)
layers.shows: Approximate places where the Corps of Discovery camped, 1803–1806. No pop-up: the symbols have no information to click.
layers.source: National Park Service, from Robert Bergantino, Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology

compellingQuestion.en: What did the Louisiana Purchase add to the United States, and why did the Mississippi River matter so much?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Qué le añadió la compra de Luisiana a Estados Unidos, y por qué importaba tanto el río Misisipi?

Open the legend: green for the land of 1783, yellow for the Louisiana Purchase.
Ask: about how much bigger did the country become?
Click inside the yellow area and read the Notes in the pop-up.
Ask: how much land was it, and what did it cost?

steps.en: Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark and use the legend.
steps.es: Abre el marcador The Louisiana Purchase (La compra de Luisiana) y usa la leyenda.

steps.en: Compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of the United States in 1783.
steps.es: Compara la compra de Luisiana, en amarillo, con el territorio de Estados Unidos en 1783, en verde.

steps.es: Haz clic en la compra de Luisiana y lee su ventana emergente.

ask.en: About how much bigger did the country become? How much land was the Louisiana Purchase, and what did it cost?
ask.es: ¿Cuánto más grande se hizo el país, aproximadamente? ¿Cuánta tierra era la compra de Luisiana y cuánto costó?

fill.en: Size: about ____ million acres. Price: $____ million.
fill.es: Superficie: unos ____ millones de acres. Precio: ____ millones de dólares.

answer.where: The Louisiana Purchase bookmark; Territorial acquisitions to 1803 layer. Legend: green = Territory of the Original Thirteen States (Ceded by Great Britain) 1783, yellow = Louisiana Purchase 1803. Louisiana Purchase 1803 pop-up, Notes: 530,000,000 acres, bought from France in 1803 for $15 million. Fill-in: 530 million acres, $15 million.
answer.accept: About double, or roughly the same size as the country before it. The pop-up's Area in Square Kilometers field confirms it: about 2.1 million km² for the purchase and 2.3 million km² for the 1783 land.
answer.text: Some edges were settled later and have their own legend entries and pop-ups: the strip ceded to Great Britain in 1818 (striped), and the parts that came with Texas in 1845 and the Mexican Cession in 1848.

questions.task: Turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio and the Missouri to name the regions, then follow the rivers on the basemap to find where their water reaches the sea, and explain why New Orleans mattered to western farmers.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds.
Click inside the large brown outline along the Ohio River and read the first line of the pop-up.
Click inside the outline along the Missouri River and read its name.
Zoom out and follow both rivers on the basemap to where their water reaches the sea.
Ask: which big river do they flow into, and which city sits near its mouth?
Ask: why did control of New Orleans matter to farmers west of the Appalachians?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds.
steps.es: En Map layers (capas del mapa), activa United States Watersheds (cuencas hidrográficas).

steps.en: Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio River and the Missouri River.
steps.es: Haz clic dentro de los dos grandes contornos marrones junto al río Ohio y al río Misuri.

steps.en: Zoom out and follow the rivers on the map to where they end.
steps.es: Aleja el mapa y sigue los ríos hasta donde terminan.

ask.en: Which river regions are the two outlines? Into which big river do they flow, and which city sits near its mouth? In 1800 farmers west of the Appalachians sent their crops to market by river: why did control of New Orleans matter to them?
ask.es: ¿Qué regiones fluviales son los dos contornos? ¿En qué gran río desembocan y qué ciudad está cerca de su desembocadura? En 1800, los agricultores al oeste de los Apalaches enviaban sus cosechas al mercado por río: ¿por qué les importaba controlar Nueva Orleans?

answer.where: United States Watersheds layer, at the bookmark's scale (zoomed out, the brown outlines are the largest regions; if the pop-up says 1 of 2, the region is the entry whose HUC ID has two digits). Pop-up, first line: Ohio Region (Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana and nearby states) and Missouri Region (the Great Plains). On the basemap both rivers join the Mississippi, which reaches the Gulf of Mexico at New Orleans; the city is not labeled, so students find the river mouth. Also accept Upper Mississippi Region or Arkansas-White-Red Region if clicked.
answer.accept: Names both regions; says their rivers flow into the Mississippi and so past New Orleans to the sea; explains that whoever held New Orleans could stop or tax western farmers' crops on the way to market, so the United States needed the port.
answer.text: Zoomed in, the layer shows smaller watersheds with their own names; ask students to zoom out until the outlines are the large regions. In 1802 Spanish officials at New Orleans stopped Americans storing goods in the port, and Jefferson tried to buy New Orleans before France offered all of Louisiana.

ask.en: Which biome covers the Great Plains? Why do you think the Corps traveled along rivers?
ask.es: ¿Qué bioma cubre las Grandes Llanuras? ¿Por qué crees que el Cuerpo viajaba siguiendo los ríos?

answer.where: Up the Missouri bookmark; Biomes layer, pop-up first line (also in the legend): Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands along the Missouri across the Great Plains. Further upriver in Montana the pop-up changes to Temperate Conifer Forests. The campsite symbols sit on the riverbanks.
answer.accept: Names the grassland biome; gives a reason for following rivers, such as travel by boat, drinking water, food, or a route through open country without roads or maps.

Follow the trail line west and point to where it leaves the yellow Louisiana Purchase.
Ask: was the Pacific coast part of the purchase?
Zoom out until the whole trail is on screen.
Open Measure and click from the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh to its western end on the Pacific coast.
Ask: how does the straight-line distance compare with the trail's 4,900 miles?

steps.es: Busca dónde sale la línea de la ruta de la compra de Luisiana, en amarillo.

ask.en: Where does the trail line leave the Louisiana Purchase? Was the Pacific coast part of it? What is the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific end of the trail?
ask.es: ¿Dónde sale la línea de la ruta de la compra de Luisiana? ¿Formaba parte de ella la costa del Pacífico? ¿Cuál es la distancia en línea recta desde Pittsburgh hasta el extremo de la ruta en el Pacífico?

fill.en: Straight-line distance: ________ miles. The trail itself is about 4,900 miles long.
fill.es: Distancia en línea recta: ________ millas. La ruta mide unas 4900 millas.

answer.where: Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark; Territorial acquisitions to 1803 layer with the legend: the trail crosses out of the yellow purchase in the Rocky Mountains (the Continental Divide, on the Montana–Idaho border) and the Pacific Northwest is unshaded, so it was not part of the purchase. Measure tool, Pittsburgh to the trail's end at the mouth of the Columbia River: about 2,200 miles (accept 2,100 to 2,300).
answer.accept: Says the trail leaves the purchase at the Rockies and the Pacific coast was outside it; a measured distance in the accepted range; may note that the straight line is less than half the trail's 4,900 miles because the Corps followed winding rivers and mountain passes.
answer.text: The basemap has no place names: Pittsburgh is where the trail line starts, at the fork where the Ohio River begins; the western end is where the line reaches the ocean.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Accept answers that give the purchase's size and price from the pop-up and use the watersheds, rivers or trail as evidence of what the land offered (rivers to the Gulf, plains, a route west) and why New Orleans and the Mississippi mattered to western farmers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; sketch pins for New Orleans and for two places on the trail, with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. The question of whose land this was is in Looking back: the map has no Native nations layer, so it is answered from Before you start (the Corps met more than 50 Tribal Nations) and reasoning, not from the map.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o ambas cosas.

objectives: Use the legend to compare the Louisiana Purchase with the land of 1783 and read the purchase pop-up for its size and price.
Use the United States Watersheds layer to name the Ohio and Missouri watersheds and trace on the basemap where their rivers reach the sea.
Follow the Lewis and Clark trail and campsites up the Missouri and use the Biomes layer to name the biomes the expedition crossed.
Find where the trail leaves the Louisiana Purchase and measure the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific coast.
Use the watershed boundaries and river routes as evidence to explain why New Orleans mattered to farmers west of the Appalachians.
discussion: The purchase pop-up gives a price and an area. Looking at the watershed layer, what did the United States actually gain control of, and why was the river mouth worth more than the land?

The map has layers for the purchase, the rivers and the expedition's campsites, but none for the Native nations who lived on and governed most of this land. Whose land was the Louisiana Purchase, and what would a layer showing them change about how you read the map?
The trail runs well beyond the yellow purchase boundary before it reaches the Pacific. Using the distance you measured and the biomes you crossed, what does the route suggest about Jefferson's goals?

differentiation.support: Do question 1 together from the front, write the three bookmark names on the board, and point out Pittsburgh and New Orleans on the basemap before pairs start question 2.
differentiation.stretch: With Biomes on, follow the trail from the Rockies to the coast, list each biome the Corps crossed, and explain how the landscape changed along the way.

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the Louisiana Purchase 1803 pop-up Notes (530,000,000 acres, $15 million) against the legend's green land of 1783, the United States Watersheds pop-ups (Ohio Region, Missouri Region) traced on the basemap to the Mississippi and New Orleans, the Biomes pop-up (Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands) and a Measure distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific of about 2,200 miles.
assessment.exemplar: The Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the United States and gave it the rivers western farmers depended on, and the Mississippi mattered because those rivers all reached the sea through New Orleans. At The Louisiana Purchase bookmark, the legend shows the green land of 1783 and the yellow purchase, and the yellow area is about the same size as the green. The Louisiana Purchase 1803 pop-up Notes say it was 530,000,000 acres, bought from France in 1803 for $15 million. When I turned on United States Watersheds, the two big brown outlines had pop-ups named Ohio Region and Missouri Region, and following those rivers on the basemap, both join the Mississippi, which reaches the Gulf of Mexico at New Orleans. That is why the port mattered: whoever held New Orleans could stop or tax farmers' crops on the way to market. At the Up the Missouri bookmark the Biomes pop-up reads Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands, and the campsite symbols sit on the riverbanks, so the new land was open plains the Corps crossed by river. Measure from Pittsburgh to the trail's end at the mouth of the Columbia River gives about 2,200 miles, less than half the trail's 4,900 miles. One limit is that the trail leaves the yellow purchase at the Rockies, so the Pacific coast was not part of what the United States bought, and the map has no layer for the Native nations who governed most of this land.

beforeYouStart.en: In 1803 the United States bought France's claim to a huge area west of the Mississippi River. Native nations lived on and governed most of that land; the National Park Service says the expedition met more than 50 Tribal Nations. President Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, to explore it and look for a water route to the Pacific Ocean. The expedition set out in 1803 and returned in 1806.
beforeYouStart.es: En 1803, Estados Unidos compró a Francia su reclamación sobre una enorme región al oeste del río Misisipi. Los pueblos indígenas vivían en la mayor parte de esa tierra y la gobernaban; el Servicio de Parques Nacionales dice que la expedición se encontró con más de 50 naciones tribales. El presidente Thomas Jefferson envió al Cuerpo de Descubrimiento, dirigido por Meriwether Lewis y William Clark, a explorarla y a buscar una ruta por agua hasta el océano Pacífico. La expedición partió en 1803 y regresó en 1806.

readingTheMap.en: The map has no place names: click an area to see its name. Use the legend: green is the land Britain gave up to the United States in 1783; yellow is the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Edges of the purchase settled later have other colors or stripes. A purple line follows the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, and small symbols mark the Corps' approximate campsites; the line and the symbols have no pop-ups. United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens and show today's landscape. Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in.
readingTheMap.es: El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares: haz clic en una zona para ver su nombre. Usa la leyenda: el verde es la tierra que Gran Bretaña cedió a Estados Unidos en 1783; el amarillo, la compra de Luisiana de 1803. Los bordes definidos más tarde tienen otros colores o rayas. Una línea morada sigue la ruta de Lewis y Clark, y pequeños símbolos marcan los campamentos aproximados; la línea y los símbolos no tienen ventanas emergentes. Las capas United States Watersheds y Biomes están desactivadas al abrir el mapa y muestran el paisaje actual.

reflection.en: The United States bought this land from France. Before you start says the Corps of Discovery met more than 50 Tribal Nations along the way. Whose land was it, and what does the map leave out?
reflection.es: Estados Unidos compró esta tierra a Francia. Antes de empezar dice que el Cuerpo de Descubrimiento se encontró con más de 50 naciones tribales en el camino. ¿De quién era la tierra, y qué deja fuera el mapa?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens; the territories, trail and campsites are on. The basemap has no place names, so students may need help finding Pittsburgh and New Orleans. The trail and campsite layers have no pop-ups.

misconceptions.claim: The United States bought the land from the people who lived there.
misconceptions.response: It bought France's claim. Native nations lived on and governed much of the land, which the United States later took through treaties and force. The map has no layer of those nations; the National Park Service says the Corps met more than 50.

misconceptions.claim: Lewis and Clark explored only the Louisiana Purchase.
misconceptions.response: West of the Rocky Mountains the trail leaves the purchase: the Pacific Northwest was not part of it.

misconceptions.claim: The Louisiana Purchase was the state of Louisiana.
misconceptions.response: It stretched from the Gulf of Mexico to British North America, covering all or part of 15 of today's states.

standards.text: Analyze the westward growth of the nation, including the Louisiana Purchase and Manifest Destiny
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
Explain major domestic and international economic, military, political, and socio-cultural events of Thomas Jefferson's presidency.
Use appropriate geographic tools and terms to identify and describe significant places and regions in American history.
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
